tagline: A wooded parkway where original bridges received their own designs.
intro: The Merritt Parkway carries Route 15 through forest, beneath elaborate overpasses and around tight curves. The Federal Highway Administration describes this 37-mile National Scenic Byway as a combination of engineering and art, singling out its Art Deco and Art Moderne bridges. It allows one hour for the drive. The parkway has two lanes in each direction, and some entrances have stop signs without a merge lane.

Built between 1934 and 1940 to relieve congestion on the Boston Post Road, the parkway faced objections from residents concerned about traffic and changes to the countryside. Planners brought engineers, landscape architects and architects together to answer those objections with a road designed for its setting. Weld Thayer Chase designed the landscape, and George Dunkelberger designed 69 bridges in a range of styles. Each original bridge had distinct decoration, though later overpasses did not all maintain that approach.

Drive east from the New York line at Greenwich through Stamford and Norwalk, then toward Westport and Fairfield. Between Westport and Fairfield lies a roughly five-and-a-half-mile stretch without an exit. Beyond Trumbull, the historic scenic corridor reaches the Housatonic River at Stratford. Nearby Boothe Memorial Park preserves a log-built toll booth removed when Connecticut abolished its highway toll booths in 1988.

moments.title: Silvermine
moments.text: Silvermine takes its name from old legends of a silver mine, although no silver has ever been found. The river supplied a more practical resource, powering twelve or thirteen mills in the eighteenth century, including tanning, lumber and spool works. In 1906, sculptor Solon Hannibal Borglum moved here and built a hillside studio. Artists gathered there to critique one another’s work, calling themselves the Knockers Club. After Borglum’s death, the group founded the Silvermine Guild in 1922; the community remains home to the Silvermine Guild Arts Center.

moments.title: The No Exit Zone
moments.text: Between Westport and Fairfield, the parkway runs roughly five and a half miles without an exit. Traffic reports call it the No Exit Zone or No Man’s Land. An interchange was planned midway along this stretch, but it depended on a northern extension of the Sherwood Island Connector. That extension never reached the parkway, and the exit was never built.

moments.title: Boothe Memorial Park, Stratford
moments.text: A wooden log toll booth gives Boothe Memorial Park a direct connection to the parkway’s past. Removed when Connecticut abolished its highway toll booths in June 1988, it is the state’s last remaining highway toll booth. Brothers David Beach Boothe and Stephen Nichols Boothe created the museum circa 1914. Its collection now comprises twenty buildings. A miniature lighthouse, windmill, carriage house and clock tower are among them. The property became a public park in 1949. Another relocated structure, Putney Chapel, arrived on the grounds in 1968 from nearby Chapel Street.
moments.notice: The preserved highway toll booth is built of wooden logs.

practical: The No Exit Zone: The parkway bars trucks, buses, trailers, towed vehicles and vehicles eight feet tall or taller because of low bridges, narrow lanes and tight curves. (checked 2026-10-11)
